answer: Diversity in Pottery Form collapsed while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increased simultaneously during the 18th century BCE to 17th century BCE transition (specifically over the 1800–1700 BCE century interval, recorded at the 1700 BCE / CE -1700 bin during the terminal Late Neolithic, directly preceding the Bronze Age). Over this interval, Pottery Form diversity (ZKeform) underwent the single steepest collapse in the entire prehistoric record, falling by ΔZ = -1.87 from +0.74 at 1800 BCE to its series minimum baseline of -1.13 at 1700 BCE. Concurrently, Pottery Decoration diversity (Zkeverz) surged by ΔZ = +1.45 from -0.48 at 1800 BCE to +0.97 at 1700 BCE. Systematic century-by-century first-difference screening across all 38 discrete 100-year transitions between 4300 BCE and 500 BCE confirms that this simultaneous divergence—where ceramic morphology sharply homogenized to baseline while ornamental decorative variety expanded—is unique to the 1800–1700 BCE century bin.

payload.hypothesis: Diversity in Pottery Form collapsed while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increased simultaneously during the 1800–1700 BCE century interval (the 18th century BCE leading into the 1700 BCE / 17th century BCE Late Neolithic horizon), marked by a ΔZ of -1.87 in form diversity down to its series floor of -1.13 and a concurrent ΔZ of +1.45 in decorative diversity up to +0.97.
payload.workflow: 1. Extracted and normalized pottery form and decoration z-scores across both capital.csv and time_series_data.csv. 2. Computed chronological forward-in-time first differences (ΔZ) across all 100-year century steps from 4300 BCE to 500 BCE. 3. Screened for instances of simultaneous negative ΔZ in form and positive ΔZ in decoration. 4. Confirmed uniqueness of the 1800–1700 BCE bin and synthesized contextual evidence from demographic and material capital indicators.
